headline: SplitMate taught you how real apps keep shared data correct: one source of truth, changes as actions, and exact money maths that you can test.

concepts.explanation: Two modelling decisions make SplitMate trustworthy. Money is stored as integer **paise**, so every sum is exact. Expenses and payments point to members by **id** (`paidBy: 'aarav'`), never by name or by a copy of the member, so there is exactly one place where a person is defined.
concepts.whyItMatters: Fintech apps from UPI wallets to Splitwise store money in minor units — a rounding bug in a money app destroys trust instantly.

concepts.explanation: `computeBalances` and `suggestSettlements` take plain data and return plain data — no React, no storage, no side effects. That makes the hardest logic in the app the easiest to reason about: same input, same output, every time.
concepts.whyItMatters: Pure business logic can be unit-tested in milliseconds and reused unchanged in a web app or a backend.

concepts.explanation: The app leans on `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and `sort` instead of manual loops. `reduce` totals the spending, `filter` + `map` + `sort` build the activity timeline, and `sort` with a comparator ranks debtors from largest to smallest.
concepts.whyItMatters: These four methods cover most day-to-day data work in JavaScript and make intent obvious at a glance.

concepts.explanation: Instead of six separate `useState` setters, every change to the group is an **action** handled by one reducer. Reading `groupReducer` tells you every way the data can change — add, delete, settle, add member, remove member — in one screenful.
concepts.whyItMatters: Reducers scale to complex state and are the same pattern used by Redux, Zustand and many production apps.

concepts.whyItMatters: Mutating state is one of the most common causes of “the screen didn't update” bugs in React apps.

concepts.explanation: Balances are **derived data**: they're recalculated from expenses and payments, never stored, so they can't disagree with the history. `useMemo` caches the result and only recomputes when members, expenses or settlements change. The context value is memoised the same way.
concepts.whyItMatters: Deriving instead of duplicating data removes a whole category of sync bugs, and memoising keeps it fast.

concepts.whyItMatters: Good validation prevents bad data from ever reaching your state — and good error messages tell people how to fix it.

quiz.question: Why does SplitMate store ₹249.75 as the integer `24975`?

codeRef.anchor: // Money helpers. Amounts are stored as whole paise (integers), never as

options: It takes less space in AsyncStorage
Integers are exact, while decimals like 0.1 can't be represented exactly in JavaScript
AsyncStorage can only store whole numbers
quiz.explanation: JavaScript numbers are binary floating point, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Integer paise add and split exactly. Storage size and formatting have nothing to do with it — AsyncStorage stores strings anyway.

quiz.question: `splitEvenly(10000, 3)` returns `[3334, 3333, 3333]`. Why not three equal shares of `3333.33`?
options: Math.floor is faster than normal division
Arrays in JavaScript can't hold decimals
React Native can't render decimal numbers
Shares must be whole paise and must add up exactly to the total, so the leftover paisa goes to the first person
quiz.explanation: Three shares of 3333.33 would add up to 9999.99 — a paisa would vanish and balances would no longer sum to zero. Giving the remainder to the first people keeps every share whole and the total exact.

quiz.question: Why does the reducer return `{ ...state, expenses: [action.expense, ...state.expenses] }` instead of calling `state.expenses.unshift(action.expense)`?

codeRef.note: The addExpense case of the reducer.

options: React compares references: a new object and array tell it the data changed, while mutating the old array can leave the screen stale
unshift doesn't exist on JavaScript arrays
Spread syntax is required inside switch statements
It sorts the expenses by date automatically
quiz.explanation: Reducers must return new state. If you mutate the existing array and return the same `state` object, React sees an identical reference and may skip re-rendering. `unshift` exists — it's just the wrong tool here — and spread does no sorting.

quiz.question: Balances are never saved to AsyncStorage. What happens to them when you delete an expense?
options: They keep their old values until the app restarts
You need to tap a Recalculate button
useBalances recomputes them from the remaining history, because `expenses` — one of its dependencies — changed
The reducer subtracts the deleted expense from each balance
quiz.explanation: Deleting creates a new `expenses` array, so the `useMemo` dependency list changes and balances are recalculated from scratch. Because they are derived, they can never disagree with the history.

quiz.question: Four roommates have non-zero balances. At most how many payments can `suggestSettlements` suggest?
quiz.explanation: Each payment brings at least one person to exactly zero, and the final payment settles two people at once. So n people need at most n − 1 payments: 3 for four roommates. Paying everyone back pairwise could need up to 6.

nextSteps.reason: computeBalances and suggestSettlements are pure functions — perfect first Jest tests, like “balances always sum to zero”.
Syncing the ledger to a backend is what lets every roommate see the same balances on their own phone.
Once data lives on a server, each roommate needs to sign in so only the room can see its money.
A gentle weekly reminder to people who owe money is the most requested feature in apps like this.
